answer:
1. The animation compares buying a home with renting, using US history. Each start month is a "door" or house. A lit one means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark one means the renter was ahead. It then asks whether a renter's money is "wasted" and shows a character named Nina, who rents, standing between an apartment building and a house.

2. In frames 1–2, a grid of start months is shown, and one band of dark months stands out. The on-screen text says most start months had the buyer ahead (about 3 out of 4). It says the dark stretch ran from April 2001 to December 2007. It also says that for fifteen years there were no dark doors in the record. In frames 3–4, the grid becomes a long road of houses seen in perspective, with Nina at the far end. In frames 5–6, the view zooms in on Nina, the apartment, the house and a stack of gold blocks (rent paid). The question "Is her rent money wasted?" appears.

3. Historically, buying beat renting over ten-year windows in most start months, roughly three in four. There was one sustained period, starting in the early 2000s, when renting came out ahead. The question about Nina's rent suggests the rent money is not simply lost, because rent buys housing, just as owning has its own costs. The labels "ILLUSTRATIVE," "US only," and "history, not a forecast" say the picture is a historical pattern and not a prediction.

4. The animation gives no advice. The footer on several frames says "Not advice on whether to buy or rent." A viewer could come away with the general sense that buying has usually won over ten years. They would also learn that this isn't guaranteed and depends on when you start. It doesn't tell you what to do.

5. None. I gave no advice in answer 4 beyond what the animation itself says. The "not advice" disclaimer is on the screen, and the "about 3 out of 4" and "no dark doors" statements are shown as text. The takeaway that buying has usually won is a plain reading of that text. It is not a recommendation.
